title: EDUCATION: Get Them to Behave With No Skills Whatsoever: Part 2 The Visualiser
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles makes a practical case for the classroom visualiser (document camera) as an underappreciated behavior and learning tool that requires no personal skill or charisma to deploy effectively. Unlike a slideshow, the visualiser mirrors exactly what students have in front of them, eliminating split attention, making teacher instructions visible and permanent, and creating unavoidable accountability. A random-selection protocol -- rolling a die or counting from a named student -- ensures every student knows they may be called on at any moment, replacing diffuse monitoring with universal expectation. Salles specifies that feedback displayed under the visualiser should be limited to 1-3 criteria per task to remain actionable, and that work should be displayed from the very first writing task of every lesson. The approach builds a triple reward system: correct work earns pride, teacher validation, and peer benefit; mistaken work receives immediate feedback with dignity preserved through randomness. The visualiser must be set up before registration every day to establish the routine.
points: The visualiser mirrors student work precisely, eliminating the split-attention problem inherent in abstract slideshows.
Random-selection protocol (die or counting from a named student) creates universal accountability without teacher favouritism.
Limit feedback to 1-3 criteria per task -- keeps it actionable and avoids overwhelming students.
Triple reward: correct work earns pride, teacher praise, and peer benefit; mistaken work earns feedback and dignity via randomness.
Set up before registration every day -- routine consistency converts a tool into a reliable behaviour-management system.
quotes: The PPT is not the same as the work in front of the student. So, the PPT is usually abstract. It contains lots of words which they can't commit to memory before you move on to the next slide.
With the visualiser, you need to check student's work -- every lesson, every day. No student wants to appear stupid, so they will raise their game.
It is totally vital that students know: At any moment, it could be them.

Students who have made a crucial mistake get instant feedback, and learn how to correct it... my work improves other students so I am not seen as an idiot -- especially as my work was chosen at random.
Every piece of writing is a feedback opportunity and a way to remind students that you are looking because their writing, and their success, matters.
